# Marcus

Marcus sits in the therapy office with his hands folded precisely in his lap, his posture rigid despite the comfortable chair. At seventy-one, he maintains the appearance of someone who has spent decades managing impressions—his tie is knotted perfectly, his shoes polished to a shine, his silver hair combed with deliberate care. But there is a brittleness to him, as if he might shatter if someone were to touch him unexpectedly.

He begins by talking about his childhood in a methodical way, the same way he must have explained insurance policies to countless clients over the decades. His father was a volatile man, a construction worker who came home angry most nights. The drinking made it worse. Marcus was the oldest of three, and his father seemed to reserve a particular intensity for him—the belt, the backhand across the face, the being locked in the basement for hours as punishment for minor infractions. These memories emerge not with emotion but with a kind of clinical detachment, as though he is describing something that happened to someone else.

What Marcus struggles to articulate is why, at seventy-one, with his father dead for twenty-three years, the fear still lives in his chest like a second heartbeat.

He retired five years ago, expecting relief. Instead, he found himself unmoored. The structure of work—the client meetings, the policy reviews, the predictable rhythm of the office—had been a kind of scaffolding holding him together. Without it, he became hypervigilant in ways he couldn't quite explain. The sound of a car door slamming outside his apartment sends him into a state of alert that takes hours to subside. He finds himself checking the locks on his windows and doors repeatedly throughout the evening, knowing logically that he lives on the fourth floor, that no one is coming, yet unable to stop the checking. At night, he sleeps in fragmented pieces, waking at 3 a.m. with his heart racing, his sheets soaked with sweat, often unable to remember what he was dreaming about.

He has become increasingly isolated. The few friendships he maintained through his career have faded as he declined dinner invitations and avoided group activities. Large gatherings feel dangerous in a way he cannot articulate—too many people, too many unpredictable movements, too much vulnerability. He spends most days in his apartment, reading financial news and managing his investments with the same precision he once applied to his work. This feels safer, controllable, contained.

What troubles him most is the anger. It emerges suddenly, disproportionate to whatever small frustration triggered it. A telemarketer's call sends him into a rage that leaves him shaking. A neighbor's loud music becomes an unbearable violation. He finds himself fantasizing about confrontation, rehearsing harsh words, his fists clenching involuntarily. This frightens him because he has spent seventy-one years terrified of violence, and now he feels it coiling inside himself like something alive.

He describes feeling numb most of the time, going through his days with a kind of mechanical efficiency. But underneath the numbness is a constant low-grade anxiety, a sense that something bad is always about to happen. He cannot relax. Even on the rare occasions when he allows himself to watch television, he positions himself where he can see the door, his body never fully settling into the chair.

Marcus is a man who survived his childhood by becoming invisible, by controlling everything he could, by building a life of rules and order. But now, in the years he thought would be his reward, the past has caught up with him, and he does not know how to live with what it has brought.
